stories.title: Digital Realty Plans 50MW Data Center for AI Workloads on Singapore's Jurong Island
stories.summary: Digital Realty is planning a 50MW data center on Singapore's Jurong Island aimed at AI workloads.
stories.why_it_matters: Jurong Island's industrial zoning and energy infrastructure offer a rare path to new capacity in Singapore's tightly controlled data center market. For operators and AI customers, expansion there signals Singapore is selectively reopening to power-hungry builds, which could reshape site selection and power allocation strategies across Southeast Asia.
stories.content:

stories.title: Whittlesea Council Seeks Greater Oversight as Dover Plans 200MW Data Center in Victoria
stories.summary: Whittlesea City Council has asked the Victorian government for greater transparency and regulation of data center developments as Dover DC's 200MW South Morang project advances through the state-led planning system. The application by Dover1 SM2 Pty Ltd for a site at 165 Williamsons Road is under state assessment, bypassing local council control.
stories.why_it_matters: The dispute highlights growing friction between state fast-track planning and community oversight as data centers push into suburban Melbourne. How Victoria resolves council concerns will set a precedent for dozens of pending projects and shape whether local pushback becomes a material permitting risk for developers.
stories.content:
Australia’s Whittlesea City Council has asked the Victorian government to improve transparency and regulation around data centre developments, as a new 200MW Dover DC project moves through Victoria’s state-led planning system in South Morang.

Dover1 SM2 Pty Ltd’s application for a data centre at 165 Williamsons Road, South Morang was received by the Victorian government on 14 August. The application is being assessed through the Development Facilitation Program (DFP) and covers the use and development of the land for a data centre, vegetation removal and signage.

Dover identifies the project as SM1B and says it will provide up to 200MW of high-efficiency infrastructure on approximately 1.8 hectares of an 8.7-hectare site next to the South Morang Terminal Station. The project is the second data centre proposed by Dover in South Morang.

### Second South Morang project

Dover’s existing SM1A project is located at 765 Plenty Road and 525–535 McDonalds Road in South Morang. The company says that facility is designed to provide up to 120MW. SM1A received planning approval from the Victorian Planning Minister in September 2024 through the Development Facilitation Program, with further amendments approved in 2025.

SM1B would therefore bring the stated capacity of Dover’s two South Morang projects to up to 320MW, assuming both are developed to their stated maximum capacities. Dover says SM1B will comprise a three-storey data hall building directly adjacent to the South Morang Terminal Station.

The Victorian government’s planning register does not disclose the project’s IT load, total facility demand or detailed electrical configuration. It currently records the application as a planning permit application under the DFP, with no decision recorded.

### Council seeks greater transparency

The new application comes as the local council for South Morang, Whittlesea Council, seeks a greater role in decisions around data centre development. In its 18 August council meeting, Whittlesea said councillors had raised concerns about the transparency, regulation and planning of data centres, and that Mayor Lawrie Cox would write to the Victorian government about the issue.

The move follows the approval of Dover’s SM1A project through the state planning system. Council was not the decision-maker for that application, which was assessed through the Development Facilitation Program.

The division of responsibility is becoming increasingly relevant as Victoria accommodates a growing pipeline of data centre projects through state-level planning mechanisms.

The issue is not confined to Whittlesea. The City of Melbourne has also begun developing a policy position on data centres and AI infrastructure, with **its draft position paper now open for consultation**. The council says many of the key decisions about data centres are made by the Victorian and Australian governments, and is seeking to influence future policy through local planning, partnerships and advocacy.

The draft position paper calls for planning controls that distinguish between different types and scales of data centres and require assessment of land use, design, amenity, energy, water, emissions, infrastructure and cumulative impacts. It also proposes consistent, comparable and publicly accessible data on energy, water, emissions, noise and backup generation.

The City is also advocating for independently assessed and publicly disclosed energy and water efficiency ratings, and for applicants to deliver and report on public benefits and respond to local needs as part of the planning approval process.

The draft position is currently out for consultation until 30 September, with a final position paper expected to return to the Future Melbourne Committee in February 2027.

### Power and water

Dover says the SM1B site has been designed around its proximity to the South Morang Terminal Station, with power, water and local amenity among the areas where it has undertaken consultation with government departments and agencies. The company says its water strategy has been developed in consultation with Yarra Valley Water and is designed around demand-management requirements.

Dover has stated a target of less than one litre of water per kilowatt-hour and says recycled water could be incorporated if an appropriate supply and connection become available. The developer has also said the project will include upgrades to the Heath’s Court Drain and improvements to the McDonalds Road frontage, including a shared-use path and widened nature strips.

Dover says the project has been designed to meet mandated noise and amenity limits, and that a noise impact assessment found noise levels within allowable limits under worst-case operating scenarios. The company says it is also undertaking further baseline monitoring ahead of regulatory requirements.

Dover currently expects construction of the South Morang project to begin in late 2026 or early 2027, subject to approvals, with initial operations targeted for late 2028 or early 2029 and capacity ramp-up continuing into 2031 and beyond.

However, detailed technical information about SM1B’s IT load, data hall configuration, cooling systems, backup power architecture and ultimate electricity demand has not yet been disclosed in the Victorian planning register.

### State planning system

The use of the Development Facilitation Program for the South Morang projects places the development within a state planning pathway rather than leaving the local council as the final decision-maker.

Victoria’s planning framework specifically identifies data centres as eligible for assessment through Clause 53.22 of the Victorian Planning Provisions where the relevant thresholds are met. The City of Melbourne’s draft position paper notes that some eligible projects can be assessed directly by the Planning Minister through the DFP.

That does not remove the ability of local councils to participate in the process or advocate on individual projects, but it means the approval pathway is ultimately determined at state level for projects proceeding through the DFP.

The Victorian Government is simultaneously developing its own Sustainable Data Centre Action Plan, covering areas including infrastructure and connectivity, energy and grid readiness, sustainable water management and government coordination.

For Whittlesea, however, the issue is now more immediate: another large data centre proposal has entered the state planning system in the same municipality where Council is asking for greater transparency and local involvement.

The SM1B application remains under assessment and no planning permit has been issued. W.Media has contacted Dover DC for comment on the new application and its engagement with Whittlesea Council.

stories.title: Korea Faces Data Center Shortage, Offering Equity Investment Opportunities for Institutions
stories.summary: South Korea is facing a data center supply shortage that is creating equity investment opportunities for institutional investors, according to Asia Business Daily coverage of AI data center investment.
stories.why_it_matters: A structural supply shortfall in Korea — driven by AI demand, power constraints, and Seoul-area permitting limits — is turning data centers into a mainstream institutional asset class there. For investors, the shortage supports premium valuations and development yields; for operators, it signals sustained pricing power in one of Asia's most supply-constrained markets.
stories.content:
## Hwawoo Alternative Investment PG Team  

Sought After by Both Domestic Institutions and Foreign Private Equity  

"Legal Counsel Essential for Managing Contract Risks"

    "In the past, data centers tended to be concentrated only in Japan due to its robust power infrastructure. As of the publication date, however, Korea ranks third globally in the fields of artificial intelligence (AI) and AI data centers, making it an attractive and well-equipped market for hyperscalers, which is leading to active investment."

Youngwoo Park, partner attorney in the Alternative Investment Practice Group (PG) at Hwawoo Law Firm, predicted that the supply of domestic AI data centers would be extremely insufficient compared to demand, and investment demand in this sector would therefore continue to increase for the next five years. However, he also advised that there are certain risks that require attention when investing, such as contractual risks with hyperscalers or risks from local civil complaints, and emphasized the importance of thorough legal consultation.

![Attorneys Sa Gongdae (from left), Youngwoo Park, and Jiwon Kwak from Hwawoo Law Firm are posing for a photo. Photo by Dongju Yoon](https://cphoto.asiae.co.kr/listimglink/1/2026081417333481769_1786696414.jpg) 

Attorneys Sa Gongdae (from left), Youngwoo Park, and Jiwon Kwak from Hwawoo Law Firm are posing for a photo. Photo by Dongju Yoon

View original image
### Trending Investments: Korea's AI Data Centers

Institutional investors are mainly investing in Korea's AI data centers through two approaches. One is acquisition of equity in data centers that have already been completed; these completed projects are mid-risk, mid-return investments where, with tenants already secured, a stable cash flow can be expected. On the other hand, development-type investments involve participating in the entire process from site acquisition, design, construction, to securing tenants. While this structure involves higher initial risks, it also allows for profitable exits by selling at higher prices after completion—making it a high-risk, high-return model. Currently, development-type investments are the dominant trend, and participation from overseas investors is particularly notable. Partner attorney Daesagong stated, "Most recent legal consulting cases involve development-type investments, and not only domestic but also many international investors are actively participating." The key advantages of Korea's AI data center investments, cited by these lawyers, are strong power and water infrastructure. Attorney Daesagong explained that, unless affected by extraordinary physical events, Korea Electric Power Corporation provides stable electricity supply, and measures such as maintaining transmission line capacity at half ensure high stability—factors positively regarded by foreign investors. In fact, Hwawoo Law Firm recently provided legal counsel on asset transfer investments involving a Singapore-based private equity fund and a listed Korean company forming a local joint venture (JV), with multiple special purpose companies (SPCs) established to participate from the earliest development stages.

![\[How to Invest in AIDCs\] "Korea Faces Data Center Shortage... Numerous Equity Investment Opportunities for Institutions"](https://cphoto.asiae.co.kr/listimglink/1/2026082017300987415_1787214610.png) View original image

The momentum behind AI data center development is now spreading to regional areas outside the greater Seoul area. Investors still prefer data centers in metropolitan regions such as Seoul and Gyeonggi Province, not only because of infrastructure but also because operation and maintenance (O&M) personnel are concentrated there. However, as new construction has become virtually impossible within Seoul due to power shortages, demand for development is shifting toward the outskirts and non-metropolitan regions. A notable example is a Singaporean fund recently making a minority equity investment in an AI data center project in Pohang, North Gyeongsang Province. Senior foreign attorney Jiwon Kwak commented that in non-metropolitan areas, the use cases for AI data centers are diversifying—for example, as backup or for AI model training—making such regions increasingly viable as data center sites. In particular, for AI model training centers, because data latency is not critical, geographic distance is less important, so there is ample opportunity for new demand outside the Seoul Capital Area.

### Are There Investment Risks? Key Contractual Points

One critical point that institutional investors must heed in development-type investments is the importance of securing end users. Failure to attract tenants such as hyperscalers—including companies like Microsoft in the United States—can result in vacancies and investment failures.

![\[How to Invest in AIDCs\] "Korea Faces Data Center Shortage... Numerous Equity Investment Opportunities for Institutions"](https://cphoto.asiae.co.kr/listimglink/1/2026082017300787414_1787214608.png) View original image

Once a tenant is secured, a "showdown" often develops between the landlord and the tenant. Whereas development companies (developers) or landlords have typically held the upper hand in traditional data center deals, for AI data centers, hyperscaler tenants now wield the dominant bargaining power. Since preventing vacancies and ensuring long-term returns depends on retaining these tenants, landlords are often compelled to accommodate end user demands. Attorney Kwak explained, "Hyperscalers will frequently present their preferred standard contracts and sometimes aggressively insist that the investor or landlord agree to their terms." These tenants frequently enforce contract provisions favorable to themselves, such as Non-Disturbance Agreements (NDA), which guarantee their rights to occupancy even in cases of changes in control or disputes.

For example, hyperscalers may include provisions in the contract allowing them to withhold rent if AI computation unit costs decline. In such cases, it benefits landlords to include a "hell or high water" clause (requiring the fulfillment of payment obligations under any circumstances) to guarantee that rent will always be paid. Another approach is to define force majeure clauses strictly: whereas hyperscalers may try to suspend rent payments or terminate contracts due to falls in AI computation prices or profitability, landlords should ensure that such commercial reasons are specifically excluded from the definition of force majeure events.

### "The Answer Is On the Ground" — Hwawoo Alternative Investment PG Team

AI data center contracts are often long-term supply agreements spanning at least 15 to 30 years after development. Throughout these periods, gray areas—issues that are hard to specify in the contract—can arise. Attorney Park noted, "In prolonged operations, it often becomes difficult to precisely delineate the responsibilities for maintenance and operation between landlords and tenants." Attorney Kwak mentioned that identifying these gray areas and mitigating the related risks is a crucial role for legal consultants.

### Hot Picks Today

!["Never Experienced This in My Aviation Career": Crew Shocked as Stranger Unexpectedly Enters First-Class Suite](https://cwcontent.asiae.co.kr/asiaresize/93/2026082416092790772_1787555368.png) "Never Experienced This in My Aviation Career": Crew Shocked as Stranger Unexpectedly Enters First-Class Suite

- Earn an Extra 870,000 Won a Month by Working After Hours in Other Departments... Japanese Company Introduces In-House Side Job System
- Lost Their Appetite at First Glance: "What's Wrong with the Naengmyeon Noodles? Truly Shocking"—AI Food Images Spark Controversy
- "I'll Serve Tuna Instead of Salmon": What Seemed Like a Windfall Had a Reason...Japanese Restaurants Shaken by Seafood Shortages
- "'Unpleasant Wind from Sweat' vs. 'What Else Can We Do in This Heat'... Subway Handheld Fan Debate Ignites First in Japan"

![\[How to Invest in AIDCs\] "Korea Faces Data Center Shortage... Numerous Equity Investment Opportunities for Institutions"](https://cphoto.asiae.co.kr/listimglink/1/2026082017301387416_1787214614.png) View original image

The Hwawoo Alternative Investment PG Team is an organization expanded and restructured in 2022 through the integration of its real estate finance and corporate crisis response teams. The team covers a broad range of alternative asset sectors, such as energy and infrastructure. Rather than simply editing contract clauses or legal opinions, they offer client-focused, field-oriented advisory services, directly communicating with clients. Attorney Park said, "We deeply understand and reflect critical conditions and industry practices—such as rent per unit of data center electrical capacity—in our advisory services." The team continues to strengthen its expertise by recruiting talent with over 10 years of experience, such as attorney Daesagong (who undertook a placement at Macquarie Capital Korea) and attorney Kwak (who specializes in cross-border practices).

stories.title: Australia to Set New Data Center Power and Water Standards
stories.summary: Australia plans to introduce new standards governing data center power and water usage.
stories.why_it_matters: National standards would move data center resource consumption from voluntary disclosure toward regulated accountability, affecting design choices, site selection, and operating costs for every operator in the country. Developers in water-stressed regions face the biggest adjustments, while early movers on efficiency gain a compliance head start.
stories.content:
## What Australia Is Trying to Do

Australia is welcoming data center investment, but it insists on guardrails. The planned rulebook extends beyond physical infrastructure. There would be one framework for the facility itself and another framework for the system operating inside it.

The pressure reflects a larger reality: data centers no longer run quietly in the background. They consume community electricity, water, and land while serving AI companies that want more capacity. A single national standard can give investors clearer expectations and give communities a baseline level of protection before a project breaks ground.

## The Energy Fight Behind the Headline

Data centers use massive amounts of power and water because they run around the clock. That makes their impact different from a typical factory. A new facility can push household bills higher if it puts the grid under strain.

As data centers strain Australia's power grids, grab the free Always Be Buying E-Book to build wealth steadily

Energy Minister Chris Bowen has been direct about what is at stake. He said the government would not permit a "race to the bottom" where states compete for data centers by sacrificing affordability, reliability, and emissions targets. On Sunday, Bowen pushed back against Queensland's objections, arguing that proper rules can attract investment without letting data centers avoid their responsibilities.

Bowen's position is that data centers should supply their own renewable power, with peaking gas plants backing them up during high demand. That approach stands sharply apart from a "build now, worry later" philosophy.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese is scheduled to address business leaders on Tuesday. His argument combines economic opportunity with public accountability. "Australia can do more to unlock frontier AI development," he says. "We must shape this change to harness the positive opportunities while minimising the downsides."

He also stresses that public support matters. "Australia is in a strong position to attract investment in data centers, but maintaining the social license will be essential," he said. "That means ensuring energy bills do not rise, water security is maintained and locations are appropriate."

## What This Could Mean for Investors

A data center appears digital, but it is deeply physical. It needs land, electricity, and water from systems that also serve daily life. If Australia requires data centers to bring their own renewable power, the project economics change before construction begins.

The AI boom has lifted utility and energy shares, but policy now decides where data centers can operate, who pays for new grid connections, and how much water they can consume. If other governments follow Australia's model of "build, but the system must hold," the AI build-out can continue but the cost will be higher.

The investment story is shifting. It is no longer only about data center growth and AI adoption. It is also about whether AI can coexist with households, farms, and fragile power grids in the physical world. The final price of that coexistence will be written in future infrastructure bills.

Australia's proposal covers one country, but the judgment is not limited to its borders. Data center investment has become a story about public policy, water, utility limits, and local pain. The next few months will show if other governments adopt the same balance between technological ambition and the physical limits of the grid.

stories.title: Beyond Power: The Search for an AI Data Center Niche
stories.summary: What makes locations ideal for AI data center needs
stories.content:
Artificial intelligence is advancing at extraordinary speed, but its physical limits are increasingly being tested by how much power can be generated, transmitted, and delivered where compute is needed.

In this context, imagine a country with abundant renewable energy, water, cool mountain air, and plenty of room to build. It sounds like an obvious place to invest.

It is not.

The AI infrastructure boom is being organized around scarcity. Power is constrained. Transmission is slow. Suitable land is contested. Cooling and water are becoming harder to secure. In that environment, a country that can offer these inputs can quickly appear to have found its opening.

But scarcity can be misleading. It makes an asset valuable; it does not make the country that possesses it strategically indispensable. The harder question is whether those physical advantages can be converted into a durable proposition, one with the capital, connectivity, institutional confidence and access to demand that investors need over decades, not merely during the current rush.

Nordic countries such as Norway and Iceland offer clean power and colder climates, advantages that energy-rich countries in South Asia, including Nepal and Bhutan, can also bring. But the propositions are not identical. The Nordics add mature infrastructure and long-established investor confidence; Nepal and Bhutan sit closer to one of the world’s most consequential future digital growth corridors.

The Gulf, Singapore and Malaysia illustrate the same point from different directions. They are building aggressively around AI not because power or land alone sets them apart, but because each combines those inputs with a distinct mix of capital, market access, connectivity, ecosystem, and institutional capacity. Power and land may help secure a project. But they do not create a niche. The question is what a country can assemble around them to create a strategic advantage.

A niche is distinctive because it survives a harder test: whether a country can combine the basic resources that make AI infrastructure feasible-energy, land, and cost-with capital, market relevance, and ecosystem to create a credible global strategic proposition. No country gains relevance simply by possessing more power, cheaper land or a colder climate. It gains relevance by assembling a combination that others cannot easily reproduce.

For countries still searching for a place in the AI economy, the lesson is not to copy an existing model. Few can replicate America’s market depth, the Gulf’s capital, or Singapore’s ecosystem. The more useful task is to turn their own physical foundation into a proposition that remains valuable as demand, technology, and energy systems evolve.

Capital and ecosystem will remain decisive. But as more governments and investors commit large sums to data centers, connectivity and technology partnerships, their presence alone will not always distinguish one destination from another. Power, land, capital and ecosystem are increasingly the conditions for entering the competition. The question is what a country can build from them.

As AI infrastructure becomes more capital-intensive and technologically uncertain, two qualities are likely to matter more in determining whether a country’s position endures: optionality and long-term relevance.

Optionality is the capacity to remain valuable across multiple future scenarios rather than depend on a single assumption about demand, technology or energy use. In the AI context, it has two dimensions. Compute optionality is the ability to serve different workloads, customers and technology cycles rather than rely on a single tenant, project or AI use case. Energy optionality is the ability to develop, control and deploy power in more than one way: through dedicated generation, grid supply, storage, flexible-load management and, where appropriate, export or other productive uses when compute capacity is not fully utilized.

Long-term relevance is a durable connection to markets or demand corridors with sustained growth potential—where demand for compute is likely to deepen over time rather than mature or saturate quickly. A country that can direct power among compute, storage and the grid—and direct compute toward AI, cloud, scientific or industrial uses—has a more resilient proposition than one dependent on a single buyer or technology cycle.

Nepal offers a useful test of this thesis. Its AI potential is often described through hydropower, Himalayan cooling, available land and lower development costs, alongside its demonstrated ability to mobilize domestic capital for large-scale hydropower. Those are meaningful foundations. But they may not, by themselves, establish Nepal as a consequential AI-infrastructure location within Asia’s rapidly expanding digital geography, particularly as India builds at far greater scale.

Nepal’s more strategic opportunity lies in what it can assemble around those foundations: energy optionality through dedicated hydropower, solar, storage and grid supply; and long-term relevance through connection to a deepening South Asian and wider Asian demand corridor. Its role would not be to replicate India’s AI build-out, but to complement it with renewable-powered infrastructure that can serve changing technologies, workloads and regional demand patterns.

For technology leaders such as the United States, this offers a useful framework. As technology companies, investors and policymakers look beyond the first wave of AI infrastructure, they will need to distinguish between countries that merely market attractive features and those that can become durable AI-infrastructure partners.

For the United States, this is also a question of diversification: whether the future infrastructure of AI will be concentrated in a small number of established markets or supported by a wider network of credible, renewable-powered partners. The question is not simply where the next data center can be built most cheaply. It is which countries can credibly host, power, finance, and sustain AI infrastructure, and the investment behind it, over time.

stories.title: Deploying 800VDC Architectures for Large-Amperage Data Centers
stories.summary: 800VDC architectures for the next generation of high-density data centers
stories.content:
![Eaton Cover 24082026_page-0001 (1)](https://media.datacenterdynamics.com/media/images/Eaton_Cover_24082026_page-0001_1.width-200.jpg) 

Higher-density compute is creating new demands on the electrical infrastructure underpinning modern data centers. As rack power requirements increase, operators need architectures that can deliver greater capacity while maintaining safety, reliability and operational resilience.

stories.title: Asia-Pacific Set for $280B Data Center Buildout: Report
stories.summary: A new report projects Asia-Pacific will see US$280 billion in data center construction spending as the region scales to meet digital and AI demand.
stories.why_it_matters: A US$280 billion buildout projection frames APAC as the world's fastest-growing data center construction market, redirecting contractor, equipment, and capital flows toward the region. It also raises the stakes on execution risk — supply chains, skilled labor, and power availability will determine which markets actually capture the spend.
stories.content:
While data centers in the US and EU face a rising wave of opposition, the Asia-Pacific is tipped to invest $280 billion in data center expansion between now and 2030.

A report by real estate consultancy Cushman & Wakefield says the region is the world's fastest-growing data center market, ranking second only to North America in installed capacity.

It is also the most underserved, with 60% of the global population but 22% of data center capacity in operation. Vietnam, the Philippines and Indonesia are among the most underserved countries.

The report said that despite 2,200MW of new colocation capacity going live in the past year, the vacancy rate had tightened, showing demand is running ahead of supply.

It said another 22.7GW of colocation capacity was in the pipeline, supported by strong pre-leasing sales, suggesting "sustained growth" in the sector over the next three to five years.

"Growth is expanding beyond established hubs such as Singapore and Malaysia into Thailand, Indonesia, the Philippines, and India, as hyperscalers and operators pursue access to power, land, connectivity, and rising domestic demand," said Vikram Kumar, head of APAC infrastructure at the International Finance Corp.

##### Government steps

But what the report, which is aimed at investors, doesn't say is that Asia-Pacific data centers also don't face the same backlash as in the US and Europe.

There have been protests and expressions of concern across the region, but nothing approaching the scale of those in the US.

According to a new poll, 75% of Americans are opposed to data center construction in their local area, with more than 60% strongly opposed. Data centers look certain to be a central campaign issue in the coming mid-term elections.

Popular opposition to data centers in the EU isn't as intense, but according to an independent count 70 projects were blocked or limited in the first quarter of the year.

One factor may be the steps already taken by governments to limit the environmental impacts.

The Singapore government imposed a moratorium on new data centers as far back as 2019 because of the demands the sector was making on its limited land supply as well as the energy and water consumption.

It lifted the moratorium in 2022, accepting proposals to build 80MW of new capacity, and last Friday gave the green light to another four companies – global players Digital Realty and Equinix and local firms Keppel Data Centers and ST Telemedia Global Data Centers (STT GDC).

They are permitted to build another 200MW in capacity and have committed to deploying green energy for more than 50% of capacity, Singapore's IMDA said.

The Singapore government is also pushing ahead with a new digital infrastructure bill that will further tighten environmental standards.

The neighboring state of Johor, the center of Malaysia's data center boom, has halted approvals for projects that don't meet power and water efficiency standards.

After absorbing US$36 billion in data center investment between 2021 and 2025, it began imposing limits last year including measures to weed out speculative investments.

In Australia, the government last month unveiled plans to require new data centers to provide their own clean energy and to limit water consumption.

After two state governments declared they would ignore the guidelines to allow for the introduction of more fuel energy, the government has accelerated the drafting of the law, with the national cabinet due to discuss it this week.

stories.title: Osaka Residents Voice Fears Over Massive Data Center
stories.summary: OSAKA - Residents in Minoh, Osaka Prefecture, have asked the city to take a more active role in explaining and reviewing plans for a large data center to be built on the former site of Osaka…
stories.content:
OSAKA - Residents in Minoh, Osaka Prefecture, have asked the city to take a more active role in explaining and reviewing plans for a large data center to be built on the former site of Osaka University's Minoh Campus, citing concerns over low-frequency noise, loss of sunlight and other potential effects on daily life.

A group of residents from the Madani residential area in eastern Minoh submitted a petition to the city on August 24, calling for explanations and verification of the redevelopment project.

The planned facility is a data center designed to handle information processing for services including generative artificial intelligence.

Data centers consume large amounts of electricity for complex computing operations and require extensive equipment to cool the heat generated by servers. They are also typically equipped with emergency generators to maintain operations during power outages.

Demand for such facilities is increasing as generative AI becomes more widely used, but data center projects have also prompted concerns among nearby residents over noise, waste heat and other environmental effects.

Similar concerns have surfaced elsewhere in the Kansai region. Video recorded three years ago in Seika, Kyoto Prefecture, showed black smoke that was said to have been emitted during testing of an emergency generator at a data center.

A resident in the area questioned the environmental impact, saying such facilities could have a significant effect on people living nearby.

In Minoh, the planned data center site lies immediately beside the quiet, green Madani residential district.

According to documents obtained by Yomiuri Telecasting Corp., two large data center buildings are planned for the former Osaka University Minoh Campus site. One of the structures is expected to be about 31 meters high, creating what residents describe as a large wall directly beside the neighborhood.

Minoh City owns the redevelopment site and selected the project operator through a public application process.

The operator has already obtained development approval and begun demolishing former university buildings. The data centers are scheduled to be completed in or after 2030.

Residents living nearby have raised concerns that the height of the planned buildings could block sunlight reaching their homes.

One resident said morning sunlight currently enters the property from the direction of the redevelopment site and expressed concern that this could be lost once the approximately 31-meter structure is built.

Others are worried about the possible effects of noise generated by the facility.

One resident said, "I am concerned about the effects of low-frequency noise on the body, such as insomnia."

The petition was submitted by the Madani residential neighborhood association, whose chairman, Uesawa, said residents want Minoh City to listen directly to their concerns and provide sufficient explanations about the project.

Uesawa said residents do not want explanations to be left entirely to ESR, the company advancing the development.

"We want Minoh City to reflect residents' opinions and listen to us," Uesawa said. "There are many voices asking the city to sincerely provide answers to residents about safety and peace of mind."

Minoh City said it would review the contents of the petition and "consider the matter sincerely."

The project operator said it has held briefing sessions and opportunities for dialogue with residents over the past several months.

"We will continue constructive dialogue with local residents while working closely with Minoh City and the relevant authorities," the company said.

Data center construction is expanding across the Kansai region as demand for generative AI and other digital services grows, bringing increasingly large computing facilities closer to residential communities.

Source: YOMIURI

stories.title: Australia's Data Center Electricity Demand Projected to Rise Sevenfold by 2036
stories.summary: Australia's data center electricity demand is projected to grow sevenfold by 2036, according to new projections.
stories.why_it_matters: A sevenfold demand increase forces grid operators, energy retailers, and policymakers to plan transmission and generation investments around data centers as a structural load rather than a niche customer. Expect intensified debate over connection queues, renewable procurement, and whether hyperscalers should fund their own power infrastructure.
stories.content:
## Data Centers as a Growing Load

Data centers never sleep. Like giant factories, they run around the clock, so they put steady pressure on a grid that has to keep supply and demand matched every second.

A terawatt-hour is a measure of electricity on a national scale, so 34 terawatt-hours is not a small jump.

That is already almost seven times today's demand.

Data centers are a tricky load because they do not ease off at night or over weekends. They run consistently across seasons, much like a large industrial plant.

That puts pressure on the grid when overall demand is lowest.

## New Demand Meets an Aging Grid

The timing is the hard part. Data centers can plug in faster than the grid can build the power lines and plants needed to serve them.

That can create bottlenecks, push up consumer prices, and force a heavier reliance on coal while new supply catches up.

As data centers' power use soars, grab the free Always Be Buying E-Book to build wealth steadily

The government wants new data centers to run on renewable power, including solar, although some regional administrators are pushing back.

AEMO chief executive Daniel Westerman says the early 2030s should be manageable. "A significant amount of new capacity is expected to be delivered between now and the early 2030s," he said.

Then he pointed further out: "Beyond 2030, the next wave of investment is critical."

Power plants are also being retired at the same time. Within 10 years, 13 gigawatts of coal and gas generation are expected to retire. That includes 2 gigawatts of capacity expected to retire in the same window.

Not every data center project will make it either.

The money is still huge. CBA estimates the data-center build-out could be worth A$150 billion by 2030.

That is the kind of scale that makes a $1 billion project look small.

What happens next depends on whether those investments land before the older plants leave. The race is between new supply and new demand.

## What This Means for Your Money

There is good news in the supply numbers.

AEMO says the new capacity has already improved the reliability outlook. That matters because reliability keeps prices from spiking when demand is high.

For investors, the more interesting story is the wave of electricity projects needed to keep up. Generation, batteries, and grid upgrades are all part of that picture.

For households and businesses, the risk is more direct. A grid stretched to serve giant power users can pass those costs along, especially during low-demand periods when data centers are doing most of the heavy lifting.

**The bottom line:** Data centers are coming either way. The question is whether the power system can scale fast enough to handle them without making electricity a lot more expensive for everyone else.

stories.title: Biological Data Center Unveils Energy Efficient AI Tech
stories.summary: A data center in Singapore has started running on human brain cells, and it isn’t a plot twist from a science fiction script. At the National University of Singapore‘s Life Sciences Institute, a…
stories.content:
A data center in Singapore has started running on human brain cells, and it isn’t a plot twist from a science fiction script. At the National University of Singapore‘s Life Sciences Institute, a working **biological data center** quietly went live on July 16, using lab-grown human neurons instead of conventional silicon chips to process information. The system was publicly unveiled on August 6, and researchers say it points toward a genuinely different way of thinking about power-hungry AI infrastructure.

Summary

## Key takeaways

- The National University of Singapore launched what its partners describe as the world’s first independently operated biologically integrated server rack.
- The system runs on 20 biological computing units containing lab-grown human cortical neurons paired with silicon microelectrode arrays.
- Each unit uses about 30 watts, compared with roughly 700 watts for a high-end Nvidia H100 GPU under full load.
- The neurons must be fed every three days and typically last around six months before needing replacement.
- DayOne, the data center operator involved in the project, is reportedly weighing a scale-up from 20 to as many as 1,000 units.

## Singapore unveils world’s first biological data center

The project is the result of a collaboration between NUS Medicine’s Yong Loo Lin School of Medicine, Melbourne-based biotech startup Cortical Labs, and Singapore-based data center operator DayOne. Together, they built what they call the first independently operated server rack powered by biologically integrated computing hardware, moving the concept out of the lab bench and into something closer to real infrastructure.

At the center of the setup are Cortical Labs’ CL1 units, each housing between 200,000 and 800,000 human cortical neurons. These cells aren’t harvested from a person; they’re grown in a lab specifically for this purpose. The neurons sit on silicon-based microelectrode arrays, creating a hybrid system where living tissue and traditional chips work side by side, each handling part of the computational load.

This hybrid approach is what makes the project notable. Rather than replacing silicon entirely, the **human brain computing** layer works alongside it, with the neurons contributing a kind of adaptive processing that conventional chips don’t naturally offer.

### Core technology and hybrid computing units

Cortical Labs previously showed that its neuron clusters could learn to play basic video games, adapting their responses to digital inputs over time. That earlier demonstration served as a proof of concept. The NUS deployment marks the first time the company A biological computing facility has been established in a location outside Melbourne’s main headquarters. The announcement of this partnership took place in March, meaning the roughly four-month gap between announcement and an operational prototype suggests the technology has moved past the purely experimental stage.

## Energy efficiency and operational specifics

The efficiency numbers behind this system are what’s drawing the most attention. Each CL1 unit consumes roughly 30 watts, life support included, while a high-end Nvidia H100 GPU can demand upwards of 700 watts under full load. That’s a difference of more than 20 times per unit, a gap that matters enormously as AI infrastructure worldwide struggles with soaring electricity demand.

That efficiency comes with a very different kind of upkeep. The neurons need feeding every three days and rely on dedicated life-support equipment that maintains precise mixtures of carbon dioxide, oxygen, and nitrogen, along with tightly controlled temperatures. Their operational lifespan runs about six months before the cells need to be replaced entirely.

### Neuron lifespan and maintenance requirements

That six-month cycle introduces a maintenance model that looks nothing like the one data center operators are used to. Conventional server hardware can run for years before it needs swapping out. Biological computing units, by contrast, require regular cell replenishment, which means ongoing costs and logistics that simply don’t exist in a traditional server room. It’s less like managing racks of hardware and more like tending a living system that needs constant care.

## Future scaling and applications

Right now, the 20-unit prototype is modest by data center standards. But DayOne, which raised **$4.5** billion in June and reached a $20 billion valuation, is reportedly considering a much larger rollout, scaling the deployment to as many as 1,000 biological computing units. At 30 watts per unit, a cluster of that size would draw around 30 kilowatts, still a fraction of what an equivalent GPU-based setup would need.

Why this matters: if the economics and reliability hold up at scale, biological computing could offer a genuinely different lever for cutting AI infrastructure’s energy footprint, rather than just incremental chip efficiency gains. A 50x jump from prototype to full deployment would be a serious test of whether the technology can move beyond a research demonstration.

### Use cases in AI processing and biomedical research

The system is designed to serve two distinct purposes. One is energy-efficient AI processing, tackling computational tasks using far less power than silicon-only setups. The other is biomedical research, including disease modeling and drug screening. Having living human neurons inside a controlled computational environment gives researchers a unique platform to observe how those cells respond to pharmaceutical compounds or simulated disease conditions, something silicon chips simply can’t replicate.

## Regulatory challenges and system limitations

Regulatory approval remains one of the biggest open questions surrounding this technology. Deploying living human tissue inside commercial computing environments raises issues that existing data center and biomedical frameworks weren’t built to handle, and any large-scale rollout will likely have to navigate rules that don’t yet fully exist.

It’s also worth being clear about what this system is not. The neurons in this **biological data center** aren’t generating consciousness or experiencing anything. They’re clusters of cells performing computational tasks, similar in function to a processor, just built from living tissue instead of transistors. That distinction matters both scientifically and ethically, and it’s central to how researchers are framing the project publicly.

### Regulatory hurdles for living tissue in data centers

As DayOne weighs scaling toward 1,000 units, the regulatory path forward will shape how fast, and how far, this kind of **energy efficient AI** infrastructure can actually grow. The next real test won’t be whether the neurons can compute, that part already works, but whether commercial and regulatory systems can adapt fast enough to let biological computing move from a single prototype rack in Singapore into something resembling standard infrastructure.

## FAQ

### What technology powers the National University of Singapore’s new data center?

It uses 20 biological computing units containing lab-grown human cortical neurons integrated with silicon microelectrode arrays, creating a hybrid system that combines **biological computing neurons** with traditional chip-based hardware.

### How energy-efficient are the biological computing units compared to traditional GPUs?

Each biological computing unit consumes about 30 watts, including life support, while a high-end Nvidia H100 GPU consumes around 700 watts under full load, a difference of more than 20 times per unit.

### What are the main challenges in operating a biological data center?

The main challenges include the neurons’ need for feeding every three days, their roughly six-month lifespan requiring periodic replacement, and the regulatory approval process for using living human tissue in a commercial setting.

### Does the system generate consciousness using human neurons?

No. The system does not generate consciousness; the neurons perform computational tasks only, functioning as clusters that process information rather than think or experience anything.

*Article produced with the assistance of artificial intelligence and reviewed by the editorial team.*

stories.title: DXN Secures AU$12.2m Contract to Deliver Containerized Data Center to HPC Customer
stories.summary: Australian firm DXN has won an AU$12.2 million contract to deliver a 2MW containerized data center to an unnamed high-performance computing customer.
stories.why_it_matters: The contract validates modular, containerized builds as a viable delivery model for HPC and edge-style demand in Australia, where speed to market increasingly outweighs scale. For local suppliers like DXN, it shows domestic AI and compute demand is creating opportunities outside the hyperscale campus segment dominated by global players.
stories.content:
Australian data center firm DXN has secured a new contract to deliver its containerized compute pods to a customer.

The company this week announced it has entered into a AU$12.2 million (US$8.7m) binding contract with an unnamed "AI compute operator" to deliver an AI High-Performance Computing (HPC) modular data center.

![DXN](https://media.datacenterdynamics.com/media/images/images_d1BdOsc.width-358.jpg) 

DXN has been tapped for the design, engineering, manufacture, delivery, installation and commissioning of a 2MW pod. The turnkey contract is for a complete 2MW AI HPC facility, combining new purpose-built DXN modules with the upgrade of existing infrastructure on site.

The customer's site is targeted to be operational in early calendar year 2027. Details on where the pods will be delivered were not shared.

Shalini Lagrutta, managing director of DXN, said: “This contract is a significant step forward for DXN. It is our second AI HPC award in as many months, materially larger than the first. This win demonstrates that the AI HPC module platform we have productised over the last three years is translating into wins across both offshore and domestic markets. Delivering 2MW of high-density GPU capacity on a single site is a meaningful uplift in scale for the product line."

She continued: "This contract will result in 2MW of high-density GPU capacity, expected to be online inside the next 12 months. DXN has been selected because the requirement is one that conventional construction cannot meet within the timeframe. This is the first phase of a potentially larger deployment, and delivering this phase well places DXN in a strong position for future phases. We look forward to delivering the project and supporting future capacity requirements should they grow."

DXN has delivered more than 100 modular data centers to date. Customers include logistics firm DP World, AngloAmerican, gold miner Newcrest in New South Wales, Stanmore Coal, as well as Boeing, Covalent Lithium, Pilbara Minerals, and satellite firm Globalstar. The company has previously delivered a number of cable landing station modules.

stories.title: FlexSysAI Launches AI Workload Orchestration Platform to Reduce Stress on the Grid
stories.summary: Will begin deployments in the Australian market
stories.content:
Nvidia-backed Australian technology firm FlexSysAI has launched a new platform to shift AI workloads across locations to reduce stress on the grid.

![flexsys-site-hero](https://media.datacenterdynamics.com/media/images/Screenshot_2026-08-24_103024.width-358.png) 

The system works by connecting live electricity market and grid conditions with AI workload balancing, shifting compute workloads to locations where power is cheap and abundant, while also allowing non-critical workloads to be reduced where necessary during periods of grid stress.

The company claims it will allow data center operators to connect to the grid sooner, lower power bills, access low-carbon power during periods of abundance, and monetize demand response services, while providing optionality over where workloads are shifted.

The platform will initially be trialed and deployed in the Australian market. The company claims to have already secured a pipeline of multiple data centers exploring adoption of the technology in Australia. It is backed by early investors EnergyLab and Sean Senvirtne, and is part of Nvidia’s Inception program.

Commenting on the launch, FlexSysAI co-founder Victor Feoktistov said: “Data centers need a strategy for the power crunch that is holding back the sector. Physical grid constraints are beginning to bite, and time to power is already a major constraint for operators. These pressures are likely to worsen over the next two to three years, while regulatory pressure is moving even faster as more jurisdictions look to require flexibility from large energy users.”

“Flexibility needs to be built into data center operations today to stay competitive. FlexSysAI can support both voluntary and mandatory approaches, but we believe giving data centers a voluntary path to participate is critical to driving early adoption. Operators stay in control, see a live price for flexibility and choose when to shift workloads, while connecting to the grid sooner and getting ahead of mandatory requirements that continue to emerge across key markets.”

FlexSysAI is one of several companies to develop a platform that can modulate AI workloads to reduce grid impact. The most notable is Emerald AI, which has developed a platform called the Emerald Conductor that mediates between the grid and data centers, orchestrating AI workloads in real time. The company has completed several demonstration projects to prove its system works within real-world data center environments. So far, it has completed two in the US, in Phoenix and Chicago, and one in the UK in partnership with the National Grid.

The company announced its first commercial project in October, with the orchestration software set to be deployed at Nvidia’s under-construction 96MW Aurora data center in Manassas, Virginia.

stories.title: Editorial: Japan's Data Center Boom Must Not Create a New Pollution Problem
stories.summary: Infrastructure development to support Japan's digital society is proceeding at a rapid pace. Measures are needed to ensure it does not create a new form of pollution.
stories.content:
(Mainichi Japan)

![](https://cdn.mainichi.jp/vol1/2026/08/24/20260824p2a00m0op014000p/6.jpg?1) 

Infrastructure development to support Japan's digital society is proceeding at a rapid pace. Measures are needed to ensure it does not create a new form of pollution.

With the spread of artificial intelligence, the construction of data centers, which process enormous volumes of information, is surging across Japan. Some estimates show that large-scale data centers have expanded about fourfold over the past seven years.

What is distinctive is that their locations are concentrated in the Tokyo metropolitan area and west Japan's Kinki region, close to the centers of demand. The reason is to avoid delays in communication, but in some cases construction is planned in front of train stations and near residential areas.

Data centers require air-conditioning equipment to cool their servers. Large-capacity storage batteries, emergency generators and fuel tanks are also installed in case of power outages. As a result, opposition movements by nearby residents concerned about noise, waste heat, fire risks and other issues have become conspicuous.

In the city of Inzai, Chiba Prefecture, a lawsuit has been filed demanding cancellation of a construction plan. The town of Seika, Kyoto Prefecture, where the municipal assembly took up the issues of noise and exhaust emissions from generators, has announced a policy of, in principle, no longer seeking to attract new projects.

Behind such distrust is the ambiguous legal status of data centers. In building confirmation applications submitted to local governments, their use is listed as "office" and other facilities. That does not match the reality of data centers that house a wide range of equipment.

These data centers are not covered by the national environmental impact assessment system, and operators have not provided sufficient information. Even basic information such as power consumption and fuel storage volume tends not to be disclosed, with security cited as the reason. This cannot dispel residents' anxieties.

Rules for construction should be clarified, including safety and environmental standards that take account of the risks posed by data centers.

Amid this backlash, industry groups are also beginning to address the issue. They have drawn up guidelines calling on operators to engage in dialogue with local residents from the site-selection stage and to thoroughly disclose information.

Overseas, regulations are advancing. In Ireland, data centers have come to account for 20% of total power consumption, and new construction in the capital was temporarily frozen. In July, the state of New York suspended for up to one year the permit process for building large-scale data centers that use massive amounts of cooling water and electricity, and indicated a policy of creating standards concerning their environmental impact and other issues.

The Japanese government intends to select candidate locations for data center clusters in various regions and accelerate development. If that is the case, it should move quickly to create a system that can win the understanding of local residents.

stories.title: Cloverleaf Infrastructure and NVIDIA Form AI Factory Development Partnership
stories.summary: US real estate developer Cloverleaf Infrastructure has formed a strategic partnership with NVIDIA, which includes a minority investment by the chipmaker. The partnership aims to support development of AI factories in the United States as demand for accelerated computing grows.
stories.why_it_matters: NVIDIA taking equity in a site and power developer shows the AI compute bottleneck has moved upstream from chips to powered land. Although the projects are US-based, the model of chip vendors bankrolling infrastructure development is one APAC markets are likely to see replicated as GPU supply chains and sovereign AI programs expand across the region.
stories.content:
Cloverleaf Infrastructure LLC (Cloverleaf), a real estate developer, has entered into a strategic partnership with NVIDIA that includes a minority investment in the infrastructure developer. The partnership is aimed at supporting the development of AI factories in the United States and Cloverleaf’s work with customers and utility partners, as demand for accelerated computing grows. NVIDIA will work with the company on infrastructure needed to develop AI factories.

According to a press release, Cloverleaf customers will have access to NVIDIA across areas including accelerated computing, high-performance networking, infrastructure and platform software, and NVIDIA DSX, under the partnership. The platform is intended to help customers weigh infrastructure tradeoffs within power, water and grid constraints. After facilities become operational, NVIDIA DSX infrastructure and software will be used to manage energy consumption and computing capacity.

![](https://w.media/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/New-Sponsor-Banner.jpg)

David Berry, Co-Founder and CEO, Cloverleaf, said, “AI is accelerating demand for digital infrastructure at an unprecedented scale and driving strong economic development opportunities for American communities, this partnership strengthens Cloverleaf’s ability to identify and develop high-quality sites that provide the compute power for our country’s growth and security.”

Nico Caprez, Vice President of Global AI Infrastructure Growth, NVIDIA, said, “AI factories are the infrastructure of the intelligence age, and land, power and shell are their foundation. Cloverleaf brings deep expertise in power and site development to create exceptional, long-lived sites for generations of accelerated computing. Together, we are accelerating the build out of AI infrastructure that will strengthen America’s energy infrastructure and power the next wave of innovation.”

J.P. Morgan Securities LLC served as exclusive financial advisor to Cloverleaf, while Kirkland & Ellis LLP provided legal counsel.

![](https://w.media/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Issue-13-Banner-1.jpg)

Cloverleaf plans to use NVIDIA’s DSX™ Platform during the design process to assess site, power, cooling, computing and facility requirements together. Access to sites with power and other infrastructure already in place is becoming increasingly important as computing demand rises.

stories.title: Zerra DC Files Plans for Large Data Center Campus in Queensland, Australia
stories.summary: Singapore-based Zerra DC has filed a development application for the Western Downs Digital Park, a 1.44GW data center campus on a 725.5-hectare site roughly 37km northwest of Dalby, Queensland. The application was lodged by project company WDDP Pty Ltd.
stories.why_it_matters: A 1.44GW proposal would rank among Australia's largest data center campuses, testing the Western Downs region's grid capacity, water resources, and planning processes. Regional councils and utilities will face pressure to accommodate hyperscale-scale loads, while developers watch whether Queensland's regional land and power advantages can attract capital away from congested Sydney and Melbourne markets.
stories.content:
A large-scale data center campus is being proposed in Queensland, Australia.

Zerra DC has outlined plans for the Western Downs Digital Park, a master-planned digital, energy, and computing hub hundreds of kilometers outside Brisbane in regional Queensland.

![zerra queensland](https://media.datacenterdynamics.com/media/images/zerra_queensland.width-358.png) 

Recently filed with the Western Downs Regional Council, the project involves the planned delivery of up to four phases of AI-ready data centers. Located on a 725.5-hectare plot 37km north-west of Dalby, roughly 250 kilometers north-west of Brisbane, the project could total more than AU$31 billion (US$22.19bn) at full build-out.

The campus is planned on land at 1933 Dalby–Kogan Road, “in proximity” to the Braemar substation and the nearby Darling Downs Gas Power Station, the Darling Downs Solar Farm, the Braemar 2 Gas Power Station, the Alinta Energy Braemar Power Station, and the Daandine CGPF.

Phase I of the campus will include the first data center (known as 1A and offering 36,000 sqm (387,500 sq ft) of data center floor space), an on-site battery-backed power conditioning system, a 540MVA substation, and supporting infrastructure. Buildings 1B, 2A, and 2B will also each total 36,000 sqm.

The dedicated project page says the site’s data centers will “utilize 100 percent air-cooled technology, removing the need for water-based evaporative cooling.”

The site is currently occupied by a 24,000-head cattle feedlot owned by the Wambo Cattle Company.

Zerra DC is a developer and operator of hyperscale data center campuses across Australia and Asia-Pacific. Owned by investment firm AGP, Zerra DC has data center developments planned across India, Japan, and Australia. The company was previously known as AGP DC.

Founded in 2018, AGP has also invested in a data center in Mumbai, India, alongside Digital Edge. The company says it has 920MW of secured capacity across the US, India, Japan, and Australia.

Zerra previously secured $127 million in funding from Tata Capital for the development of another data center in Navi Mumbai, India. The firm is also eyeing a former automotive plant site in Melbourne, Australia, for a potential data center development.

Australian industry body, the Queensland Renewable Energy Council (QREC), said the Western Downs campus proposals demonstrate how the region’s diverse energy mix and strong agricultural base are “strengthening its appeal to major new energy-intensive industries.”

“The Western Downs has long been one of Queensland’s great energy-producing and agricultural regions, with established coal and gas industries sitting alongside grain, cotton, feedlots and other agricultural production,” said Katie-Anne Mulder, CEO, QREC.

Vietnam's data center accelerator market is projected to reach USD 4,193.7 million by 2030, growing from USD 1,389.5 million in 2025.

Vietnam's data center accelerator market is expected to grow at a compound annual growth rate of 24.7% between 2025 and 2030.

Vietnam's market growth is driven by hyperscaler investments, government digital transformation initiatives, increasing AI and machine learning adoption, and the country's strategic position as a regional technology hub.

Vietnam's 24.7% CAGR significantly exceeds the global data center accelerator market CAGR of 16.9%, reflecting stronger regional demand and infrastructure expansion.

Primary applications include AI workloads, machine learning inference and training, high-performance computing, cloud services, and enterprise digital transformation initiatives across Vietnam.

The research study involved four major activities in estimating the size of the data center accelerator market. Exhaustive secondary research has been done to collect key information about the market and peer markets. The next step has been to validate these findings and assumptions and size them with the help of primary research with industry experts across the value chain. Both top-down and bottom-up approaches have been used to estimate the market size. After this, the market breakdown and data triangulation were adopted to estimate the market sizes of segments and sub-segments.

In the secondary research process, various secondary sources were referred to identify and collect information required for this study. The secondary sources include annual reports, press releases, investor presentations of companies, white papers, and articles from recognized authors. Secondary research has been mainly done to obtain key information about the market’s value chain, the pool of key market players, market segmentation according to industry trends, regional outlook, and developments from market and technology perspectives.

The data center accelerator market report estimates the global market size using the top-down and bottom-up approaches and several other dependent submarkets. Major players in the market were identified using extensive secondary research, and their presence in the market was determined using secondary and primary research. All the percentage shares, splits, and breakdowns have been determined using secondary sources and verified through primary sources.

Extensive primary research has been conducted after understanding the data center accelerator market scenario through secondary research. Several primary interviews have been conducted with key opinion leaders from demand- and supply-side vendors across four major regions—North America, Europe, Asia Pacific, and RoW. Approximately 25% of the primary interviews have been conducted with the demand-side vendors and 75% with the supply-side vendors. Primary data was collected mainly through telephonic interviews, which comprised 80% of the total primary interviews; questionnaires and emails were also used to collect the data.

After successful interaction with industry experts, brief sessions were conducted with highly experienced independent consultants to reinforce the findings of our primary research. This, along with the in-house subject matter experts’ opinions, has led us to the findings as described in the report.

Note: “Others” includes sales, marketing, and product managers

In the market engineering process, the top-down and bottom-up approaches and data triangulation methods have been used to estimate and validate the size of the data center accelerator market and other dependent submarkets. The research methodology used to estimate the market sizes includes the following:

- Over 35 companies offering data center accelerators were initially identified, and their offerings were mapped by type, processor type, vertical, and function.
- The market was segmented based on the collected primary and secondary data to reflect the distribution of different accelerator types across industries and functions.
- Global server shipments for top players in each processor category were tracked, and a suitable penetration rate was applied to estimate the number of deployed data center accelerators.
- The market value for each processor type was calculated using the average selling price (ASP), obtained from secondary sources and validated through primary interviews.
- CAGR estimation was performed by analyzing industry penetration rates and demand-supply dynamics across verticals and deployment functions.
- Data sanity checks were conducted by reviewing the revenues of over 35 key providers via annual reports, press releases, and public filings, with each company’s revenue weighted according to its data center accelerator portfolio.
- All estimates were cross-verified with key industry stakeholders, including CXOs, directors, and operations managers, and further validated by MarketsandMarkets domain experts.

After arriving at the overall market size by the market size estimation process explained in the earlier section, the overall data center accelerator market has been divided into several segments and subsegments. The data triangulation and market breakdown procedures have been used to complete the overall market engineering process and arrive at the exact statistics for all segments, wherever applicable. The data was triangulated by studying various factors and trends from the perspectives of demand and supply. Along with data triangulation and market breakdown, the market has been validated by top-down and bottom-up approaches.

Data center accelerators are specialized hardware modules that enhance CPUs, offering higher throughput, lower latency, and improved energy efficiency for AI training and inference, HPC, analytics, and infrastructure offload. Key types include GPUs, CPUs, FPGAs, and ASICs. The market is evaluated across data center types, functions, processor types, verticals, and regions. The forecasts are supported by vendor strategies, hardware-software integration, performance-per-watt improvements, and supply chain factors. Growth is due to the AI adoption, rising data volumes, and demand for scalable, low-latency computing, with opportunities in hybrid deployments and energy-efficient designs. Leading players include NVIDIA Corporation (US), Advanced Micro Devices, Inc. (US), Intel Corporation (US), Alphabet, Inc. (US), and Amazon Web Services, Inc. (US).
